title: The half-golden mongoose
hookLine: a mongoose, half gold, rolls through a king's great sacrifice and says it isn't enough
carry: dana: a gift is weighed by what it costs
tomorrow: the second road: what is bhakti, the path of love?
last: THE WORLD IS A DOG'S CURLY TAIL.

lines: NOT EQUAL TO A LITTLE FLOUR.
cards: The great war of the Mahabharata is over. The winner, King Yudhishthira, holds an enormous sacrifice to mark his reign: gold for the priests, food for the crowds, gifts on every side.
Then, in the middle of the ceremony, a mongoose runs in. Half its body is ordinary brown fur. The other half shines like gold.
It rolls on the ground, gets up, looks at itself, and says: this great sacrifice isn't equal to a little barley flour once given by a poor family. Everyone goes quiet. What family?

teach.b: The mongoose tells them. There was a famine. A poor brahmin lived with his wife, his son and his son's wife, and for days they'd had nothing.
At last they got a little barley flour, just enough for four small portions.

teach.h: EACH ONE GIVEN TO A GUEST.
teach.b: They were about to eat when a guest came to the door, starving. The father gave his portion. The guest was still hungry.
The wife gave hers. Then the son. Then the daughter-in-law.
The guest ate, and revealed himself: he was Dharma, the god of righteousness himself, and he blessed them.

teach.h: THE GRAINS THAT TURNED TO GOLD.
teach.b: The mongoose had come out of its hole and rolled in the few grains left on the floor, and wherever the flour touched, it turned to gold.
Ever since, it's gone from sacrifice to sacrifice, rolling on the ground, looking for another gift that great, to turn the other half gold. It still hasn't found one.
Vivekananda retold this story in his talks on karma yoga. The point isn't that kings shouldn't give.

teach.h: DANA: WEIGHED BY WHAT IT COSTS.
teach.b: It's how Hindus weigh dana, giving: not by its price, but by what it costs the one who gives, and how freely it's given. That's where the week has been going. Arjuna's dropped bow: every act an offering.
Janaka: unattached. The birds and the butcher, each great in their own place. Your own work as worship.

teach.h: A GIFT IS WEIGHED BY WHAT IT COSTS.
teach.b: And now: the smallest gift, fully given, outweighing gold.

how: Hindu teachers often retell the Mahabharata's story of the half-golden mongoose to explain that the worth of a gift, a sacrifice or a day's work lies in how freely and fully it's given, not in its size.

o: barley flour, the poor family's whole gift
clarified butter poured into a sacred fire
a gold coin given at a king's great sacrifice

games.q: the week of karma yoga — tap the pairs.
p: every act can be an offering
do the work, don't be owned by it
your own duty, done with care, is worship
a small gift that outweighs gold

s: the mongoose says the king's sacrifice was the greatest it had seen
it says the great sacrifice wasn't equal to a poor family's little barley flour.
in the story, the guest turns out to be Dharma himself
the hungry guest reveals himself as Dharma, and blesses the family.
the story teaches that kings shouldn't give
it teaches that a gift is measured by what it costs the giver and how freely it's given.

games.q: a rich donor gives thousands to the temple; a student gives twenty dollars she earned babysitting. by the mongoose story, how is a gift weighed?
o: by its size: the biggest gift is the greatest.
by what it costs the giver, and how freely it's given.
by whose name gets read out.
games.why: a poor family's last barley flour outweighed a king's great sacrifice. dana is weighed by what it costs, and both gifts can be real.

practice: Look back over the week and let each picture pass with a breath: the bow on the chariot floor, the city on fire, the birds and their fire, the butcher feeding his parents, the first roti, the curly tail, the mongoose.
Then ask: what's one small thing I gave this week that nobody saw? Don't grade it, just notice it was given; if you pray, offer the whole week as it was, and if not, rest in it.

wordCard.voice: Saktu, barley flour, the poor family's whole gift. Dana, giving, is weighed by what it costs the giver and how freely it's given. Small gifts can outweigh gold.

orig.note: Sanskrit: saktu, barley flour or meal; the poor family's whole gift in the Mahabharata's mongoose story.

carryVoice: Your line: dana: a gift is weighed by what it costs. Tomorrow, a new road: devotion. That's the karma week, finished.

sources.ref: Mahabharata, Ashvamedhika Parva (the mongoose and the barley-meal gift, after Yudhishthira's horse sacrifice)
Swami Vivekananda, Karma Yoga (1896) (his retelling of the mongoose story)
